The Senate on Tuesday warned that political candidates whose supporters instigate or participate in electoral violence risk disqualification, irrespective of party affiliation, as it moved to check escalating attacks on political leaders and supporters ahead of the 2027 general elections.
The upper chamber urged the Independent National Electoral Commission (INEC) to enforce the relevant provisions of the 2026 Electoral Act against electoral offenders, stressing that political violence must attract appropriate sanctions.
It also called on the Nigeria Police Force and other security agencies to investigate reported attacks on the convoys of President Bola Tinubu, presidential candidate of the Nigeria Democratic Congress (NDC), Peter Obi, and former Vice-President Atiku Abubakar, identify their perpetrators and sponsors, and ensure their prosecution.
The resolutions followed a motion sponsored by Senator Abdul Ningi (ADC, Bauchi Central), titled: “The Urgent Need to Check the Rising Incidence of Political Violence, Intolerance and Attacks on Political Leaders and Supporters in Nigeria.”
Leading the debate, Ningi expressed concern that the growing wave of political violence posed serious threats to national security, democratic participation and the peaceful conduct of the January 16, 2027 presidential and National Assembly elections.
He recalled the reported attack on Tinubu’s convoy shortly after the president observed Jumu’ah prayers at the Shehu Shagari Central Mosque, Garki, Abuja, on Friday, November 13, when the departing convoy was allegedly pelted with stones and other dangerous objects, damaging vehicles and injuring security operatives.
The senator also cited the reported attack on Obi and other political stakeholders during a political gathering in Edo State, the violent disruption of an NDC and Obidient Movement procession in Asaba, Delta State, on November 7, which reportedly left one person dead and five others injured, and the reported attack on Atiku’s convoy in Sokoto State.
He warned that failure to investigate and prosecute those responsible could embolden further attacks, deepen political divisions and undermine public confidence in the electoral process.
Seconding the motion, Senator Ali Ndume (Borno North) described the attack on Tinubu’s convoy as an embarrassment to the country rather than the president.
“What happened to Mr. President is not an embarrassment against the president; it is an embarrassment to Nigerians. On a Friday, in a mosque, it is wrong,” he said.
Ndume warned that political violence could escalate if decisive measures were not taken, urging the police to prohibit dangerous weapons during campaigns and prosecute anyone caught carrying knives and other harmful objects.
He also proposed special courts to ensure speedy prosecution of electoral offenders.
However, Senator Kawu Sumaila (Kano South) argued that political candidates should equally be held accountable when their supporters are found carrying dangerous weapons.
“It is across all parties. You see candidates with police escorts and thugs. Let the candidates be prosecuted if their supporters are found with dangerous weapons,” he said.
Sumaila also proposed reducing the reporting period given to the relevant Senate committees from four weeks to one week.
Senator Abba Moro (Benue South) maintained that existing provisions of the Electoral Act were sufficient to address electoral violence if properly enforced.
“We have various sections in the Electoral Act to tackle election violence. We need to urge the security agencies to prosecute,” he said.
Moro warned that unchecked violence could discourage citizens from participating in the elections.
“If this is not nipped in the bud, then certainly, our election and electoral process will be in danger. It will cause voter disenfranchisement; voters will be so scared even to vote. What then will become of our democracy?” he asked.
Senator Babangida Hussaini (Jigawa North-west) urged INEC to disqualify candidates linked to political violence, while Senator Binos Yaroe (Adamawa South) called on state governors to guarantee opposition parties access to public facilities for political activities, including campaign rallies.
Adopting the motion, Senate President Godswill Akpabio urged the federal government to direct the Inspector-General of Police, Olatunji Disu, and other security agencies to strengthen security arrangements for political leaders, candidates, supporters and political gatherings nationwide.
He also called for effective early-warning and rapid-response mechanisms to prevent attacks before they occur.
Akpabio specifically urged INEC to implement the relevant provisions of the 2026 Electoral Act, warning that candidates and supporters found to have instigated violence must face the consequences prescribed by law.
He said the provisions should apply without discrimination, regardless of the political party involved.
The Senate further urged state governors to stop denying opposition parties access to public facilities, including hotels and stadia under their control, for legitimate political activities, warning that such restrictions could undermine the level playing field required for credible elections.
It mandated its Committees on National Security and Intelligence, Police Affairs, and INEC to engage relevant institutions and report to the chamber within four weeks on measures to prevent political violence and safeguard the 2027 general elections.
The Senate’s intervention comes amid growing concerns over violence accompanying political campaigns across the country.
The National Peace Committee, chaired by former Head of State, General Abdulsalami Abubakar, recently reported 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord across 26 states and the Federal Capital Territory between August 19 and October 27, 2026.
Political violence and thuggery accounted for 33 of the reported violations.
Similarly, the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data (ACLED) project documented more than 30 attacks targeting political campaigns, candidates, supporters, convoys and gatherings since presidential and National Assembly campaigns commenced on August 19, with more than 10 deaths and several injuries recorded.
